nameStory: This tiny scarlet cup earned its whimsical name from its brilliant red, cup-shaped form that looks like it could serve as a drinking vessel for woodland elves. The 'scarlet' part is obvious once you spot one - these little fungi glow like tiny red lanterns against the winter forest floor. Early naturalists must have imagined these magical-looking cups belonged in a fairy tale!
description: The Scarlet Elfcup is a small, cup-shaped fungus that brings a splash of brilliant red color to the winter woods. These little fungi typically measure about half an inch to an inch across, forming perfect shallow cups or bowls. They're what scientists call 'saprobic,' meaning they feed on dead organic matter, helping break down fallen branches and woody debris. Despite their delicate appearance, they're surprisingly hardy, often popping up during mild spells in winter and early spring.

idTips.label: Brilliant Red Cup Shape
idTips.description: The most striking feature - a vivid scarlet red cup or shallow bowl, smooth and waxy to the touch, that catches your eye from several feet away

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Typically ranges from a quarter-inch to about an inch across - small enough to fit on your thumbnail to the size of a bottle cap

idTips.label: Smooth Interior Surface
idTips.description: The inside of the cup feels smooth and slightly waxy, like touching a candle, with an almost glossy sheen that reflects light

idTips.label: Growing on Dead Wood
idTips.description: Always found sprouting from decaying hardwood branches, twigs, or bark - never growing directly from soil

idTips.label: Winter Appearance
idTips.description: One of the few colorful fungi you'll find in winter, often emerging from snow-covered or frost-touched wood

habitat: Look for Scarlet Elfcups in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly on fallen branches and twigs of hardwood trees like oak, maple, and beech. They prefer moist, shaded areas where dead wood stays damp, such as forest floors near streams or in protected valleys. You'll often find them on wood that's been on the ground for a season or two - not freshly fallen, but not completely decomposed either.

seasonality.spring: Prime season for elfcups - they become more numerous as the weather warms and moisture increases, often appearing in small clusters on the same piece of dead wood.
seasonality.summer: Less common during hot, dry periods, but can still be found in consistently moist, shaded locations where their woody substrates don't dry out completely.
seasonality.fall: Begin appearing again as autumn rains return moisture to the forest floor and temperatures cool, often continuing to fruit into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Remarkably, these hardy fungi can appear during winter thaws and mild spells, creating stunning red splashes against snow-covered logs and bare forest floors.

funFact: Scarlet Elfcups are like nature's antifreeze containers - they can actually survive being frozen solid and continue growing when they thaw out, which is why you might discover these brilliant red cups emerging from snow-covered logs on a winter hike!
confusionNotes: The main confusion is with other red cup fungi, but Scarlet Elfcups are distinguished by their smooth, waxy interior and preference for hardwood. Remember: 'Smooth scarlet cups on sticks' - if the interior is rough, wrinkled, or growing on conifers, it's likely a different species.
contextualKnowledge: There are actually several very similar scarlet cup species that even experts struggle to tell apart without microscopic examination, so don't worry if field guides seem to show slightly different versions - they're all part of the same close-knit family of winter-loving red cups.
compareHints: Scarlet Elfcup is nearly identical to its close relatives like Scarlet Cup and the stalked scarlet cup, with differences mainly visible under a microscope. The stalked scarlet cup tends to have a more obvious stem, while Scarlet Cup may appear slightly more orange-red, but in the field these distinctions are often impossible to make reliably. All share the same brilliant color, cup shape, and preference for dead hardwood.
